steps.title: A worked example: Rhodamine 6G in water
steps.text:
We will work one concrete case all the way through, and you will end up with a number you can use.

The sample: Rhodamine 6G in water at 25 °C, on a confocal microscope with a 488 nm laser.
The question: at the power I normally use, how badly does my FCS fit overestimate the concentration?

Start by selecting Rhodamine 6G (3-state, triplet) in this box.

steps.title: Step 1 — the laser line: type 488
steps.text:
Set the excitation wavelength to 488 nm.

This is not cosmetic. The wavelength fixes the photon energy, so it decides how many photons per second a given power actually delivers — the same 1 mW is 33 % more photons at 650 nm than at 488 nm. Set it before the extinction coefficient, because ε is read at whatever wavelength is showing here.

steps.title: Step 2 — ε at 488 nm, not ε at the peak
steps.text:
Rhodamine 6G absorbs maximally near 530 nm with ε ≈ 116 000 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, but we are exciting at 488 nm, where it is roughly 100 000 M⁻¹cm⁻¹.

If your dye is in the repository, pick it here and ε(488 nm) is read straight off its stored absorption spectrum. If it is not listed, leave this empty and type 100000 into the ε row of the Optics & measurement table next to the state diagram.

Using the catalogued peak ε instead is the most common way to get an excitation rate badly wrong — for a dye excited well off its maximum it can be a factor of hundreds.

steps.title: Step 3 — the optics: w_r = 250, w_z = 1000, D = 400
steps.text:
In the Optics & measurement table beside the state diagram, set:
• wr = 250 nm and wz = 1000 nm — your beam waists, calibrated from a dye standard at low power.
• D = 400 µm²/s — Rhodamine 6G in water at 25 °C.

With these, the unsaturated diffusion time is wr²/4D ≈ 39 µs. Keep that number: everything below is measured against it.

steps.title: Step 4 — set the power to 0 and see the baseline
steps.text:
Type 0 here.

The red saturated curve lands exactly on the blue unsaturated one, and the summary reports Veff/V₀ = 1.000. That is not an approximation or a limit: with no excitation there is no populated scheme, so the model returns the analytical Gaussian.

This is your reference. Now we break it.

steps.title: Step 5 — 50 µW is already not a low power
steps.text:
Now type 0.05 mW — 50 microwatts, a power most people would call gentle.

Read the summary: the peak focal rate is kexc(0,0) ≈ 48 µs⁻¹ against a fluorescence decay rate of 250 µs⁻¹, so the molecule is already spending a fifth of its time unable to absorb. The result:
• Veff/V₀ ≈ 1.33 — a fit would report 33 % too many molecules
• τD ≈ 47 µs instead of 39 µs

Nothing about the sample changed. Only the lamp.

steps.title: Step 6 — 2 mW, and the damage is threefold
steps.text:
Type 2 mW.

• Veff/V₀ ≈ 3.3 — the concentration is now overestimated more than threefold
• τD ≈ 87 µs, over twice the true 39 µs, so an apparent D less than half the real one
• the amplitude G(0) has fallen to ~30 % of the unsaturated value

Every one of those biases points the same way, and none of them announces itself: the curve still looks like a perfectly good FCS curve and still fits beautifully.

steps.title: Step 7 — watch where it goes wrong, in space
steps.text:
Toggle the state populations on and look at the Profiles panel.

The cyan curve is the excitation rate — still a clean Gaussian. The yellow curve is the emission F(r) = Σ Qi Pi(r), and it is not: it has a flat top, because at r = 0 the molecule is either already excited (green, S1) or parked in the triplet (purple, T1).

That flat top is the whole story. A wider emission profile is a bigger Veff, and Veff is what sets G(0).

steps.title: Step 8 — pick your operating power
steps.text:
Look at Volume(P): Veff/V₀ against power, with your current power marked in red. For this dye and this waist there is no flat region above ~10 µW — which is the honest answer to "what power is safe?".

So the defensible protocol is a power series extrapolated to zero, not a correction factor. Use this plot to choose the powers to measure at, and use Veff/V₀ to know how much you are correcting.

Finally, tick this box to normalise G(0) = 1 and compare the shapes: the saturated curve is not just smaller, it is broader.

steps.title: Now make it your dye
steps.text:
Everything above was three arrays, and none of them assumes a triplet:
• Kdark[to, from] — here k21 = 250 /µs (a 4 ns lifetime), k23 = 2.5 /µs (1 % ISC yield), k31 = 0.5 /µs (a 2 µs triplet).
• Kexc[to, from] — σ12 = 1.
• Q — only S1 emits.

Raise Number of States to add a photo-isomer or a bleached state; double-click a rate badge on the diagram to edit it; 💾 saves the scheme as JSON so your dye's photophysics is reusable. Try the Cyanine 5 preset to see what happens when the dark state relaxes on the diffusion timescale rather than well below it.
